features.description: Ongunnon, began, takes the three infinitives onwinnan, attack, niman, take, and hęrgian, plunder. Pihtas are the Picts, Scottas the Scots; norðan and westan mean from the north and from the west. Hīe refers to the Britons introduced in the separate context; ǣhta means possessions.

features.description: Iermdon and hīendon mean afflicted and oppressed. Fela gēara means for many years, with genitive after fela. Hīe can be the Britons as object with the raiders continuing as subject, or the raiders as subject with a Briton object understood; the events do not change. Do not infer a unique case from the spelling.

features.description: On ðǣre unstilnesse, amid that unrest. Onsęndon is the exact prefixed sent; the Britons are now the subject. Ǣrendwrecan, messengers; tō Rome, to Rome. Mid gewritum and wēpendre bēne means with letters and a tearful petition. Wēpendre is a present participle, strong dative feminine singular agreeing with bēne.

features.description: In him fultumes bǣdon, him names the Romans asked and fultumes is the genitive thing requested: help. Hīernes is obedience; singāl is continual; underðēodnes is subjection. Ēaðmōde and singāle are accusative feminine singular. The promise is made by the Britons to the Romans.

features.description: Gefultumoden is a preterite subjunctive: if they, the Romans, would help them, the Britons. The following ðæt clause gives the purpose, so that they might overcome their enemies. Meahten is the known preterite subjunctive plural of magan; oferwinnan means overcome. This whole reported condition/purpose sequence is supported locally.

features.description: Here the subject of onsęndon is the Romans, while him refers to the Britons. Tō fultume means as help/to their aid. The Old English says they sent an army in the active voice; Cook compares a passive Latin expression. Preserve the actual Old English voice when analyzing it.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Sōna ðæs-ðe means as soon as. On ðis īgland has the accusative goal, to/onto this island. Hīe refers to the Roman force. The following ðā resumes the narrative.

features.description: Campedon, fought; wið hiera fēondum, against their enemies, with the source dative after wið. Him micel wæl ongeslōgon means inflicted great slaughter on them. Of hiera gemǣrum means out of their borders, with dative after of; the borders belong to the Britons, Rome’s allies. Āflīemdon means put to flight, reinforcing ādrifon. The enemy object carries on through the coordinated verbs.

features.description: Lǣrdon means advised/instructed. Fæsten is a fortification; worhten is the known unprefixed wyrcean preterite subjunctive, here make/build in the advice clause. Him tō gebeorge means for their own protection. The Romans give the advice and the Britons are to build. The source’s wið + dative remains locally supplied.

features.description: Sige means victory. Mid micle sige is with great victory: the adjective has the instrumental micle beside the dative noun, as Cook’s note directs. Treat this as a supplied source construction. Hām is the directional home, without a preposition.

features.description: Read the three ðā forms in order as when, then, the. The first ðæt is an anticipatory object, this/that, expanded by the later that-clause. Ongēaton means realized; ǣrran gewinnan means former enemies. Gewinnan is a weak masculine plural noun, distinct from the previously supplied neuter gewinn, trouble.

features.description: Rōmanisca is the weak masculine adjective Roman. Wæs onweg gewiten means had gone away: gewiten is the past participle of intransitive gewītan. This is an intransitive completed-state/perfect expression, not a passive. The source has plain-e onweg; retain it beside the earlier selected onwęg.

features.description: The returning subject is the Picts and Scots. Sōna means immediately; mid sciphęre, with a fleet. On hiera landgemǣru has accusative plural for movement into their territory; the territory is the Britons’.

features.description: Cwealdon means killed. Slōgon and cwealdon reinforce the attack. Ealle is all, naturally people in context; the following neuter ðæt is a headless/collective all that they encountered. A translation all they encountered need not pretend that ðæt is an overt masculine personal relative. Cook’s Latin note reads cædunt.

features.description: Swā-swā means just as/like. Rīpe ierðe means ripe crops, a collective feminine accusative phrase. Fortrǣdon, trampled down; fornōmon, destroyed/laid waste. The Britons are treated as a crop that is trampled; the object continues from the preceding clauses.

features.description: Foriermdon means ruined/reduced to misery. Hīe is the Britons as object. Mid ealle is the fixed phrase completely/utterly; ealle is instrumental here. The complete phrase is supplied.
